items.html: Licence plates in Brazil were white until 2018. Now, a white plate with a blue stripe on top is used. Red is still used for commercial vehicles.

Portuguese is spoken in Brazil, as opposed to most Latin American countries which speak Spanish. Compared to Spanish, some essential differences are that Portuguese uses -ão rather than -ón, -ch/-lh instead of -ll and -nh instead of -ñ.

Soil in most of Brazil is distinctly red. It can range from a light pink around Mato Grosso to a deep maroon near the Paraná river. The soil is usually not red in the North East, or in the majority of Rio Grande do Sul, however.

NOTE: Parts of Paraguay and the nearby Argentine province of Misiones have deep red soil, as well a handful of other regions around the world.

The most common poles in Brazil have some resemblance to a ladder in the bottom portion. They are rectangular, have long segments running through the bottom, and small holes near the top.

NOTE: Paraguay uses similar poles.

Most Brazilian road signs have the backs painted black.

NOTE: This is also common in Paraguay.
Blue road markers with the road number and kilometre can be seen on the sides of roads.
Brazil uses yellow on black chevrons, as opposed to most of South America, which use black on yellow chevrons.
Roads in Brazil will usually feature double yellow middle lines, with white outer lines. Roads can occasionally have a single dashed yellow line.
There are frequently white painted kerbs on Brazilian roads.
Many houses throughout Brazil have orange tiled roofs.
It is fairly common to see transparent satellite dishes, which within Latin America is generally unique to Brazil.
Blue Fortlev water tanks are often seen on Brazilian roofs.

In Generation 3 coverage, you can see two different cars:

  • A white car with a stubby antenna. There is a diagonal coil wrapped around the antenna.
  • A white car with no antenna.

The car’s colour is not always visible, meaning you will often see either just the stubby antenna, or no hints of the car at all.

The stubby antenna with a diagonal coil can also be found in Ecuador, Colombia, and Mexico.

The Generation 4 cars you can find in Brazil have a visible front, and have one of the following three colour patterns:

  • Blue
  • White with a blue stripe
  • White

Brazil also has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front.

NOTE: Brazil, Peru, Uruguay and Argentina are the only South American countries with smallcam.

Most of the coverage in Brazil is along the eastern half, with only sparse coverage in the Amazon.

It is useful for beginning players to start forming a rough mental map of where the (limited) coverage is in the western half. When you get Amazonian rounds, this can prevent you from wildly plonking hundreds of kilometres away from the nearest road.

Area codes are common to see in Brazil. They are often notated using parentheses, or at minimum as two separate numbers. Phone numbers are sometimes without area codes, and without them will be 8 numbers long for landline and 9 for mobile.

The pattern for each of the states is very learnable and useful. The area codes are grouped by first digit, so even just learning those can already help a lot. Notably, area codes ending in 1 will always be around major cities and state capitals.

Each Brazilian state has a two-letter acronym. These show up most prominently in the numbers of state roads (found on kilometre markers). They can also be found in other contexts however.

The state acronyms show up when you zoom out a little bit on Google maps, which is also possible in the minimap while in-game. However, for quick and or competitive games, it can be very useful to learn them by heart anyway, as this can help a lot with eliminating scanning time.

Postcodes (CEP) are seen frequently on street signs in Brazil (though sometimes hard to read). The first two numbers will depict an area, a state or multiple states. The numbers go anti-clockwise from São Paulo, ending in Rio Grande do Sul.

Shown here is an elevation map of Brazil. It can help to have a rough mental map of where you can find mountains, and which regions are more flat. The highest mountains are generally found near the southeastern coast.
Northeastern Brazil can be identified by its dry soil, shrubs and succulents (the Caatinga landscape). In rainy season coverage, the shrubs are still recognisable, but can be deceptively green.

The Amazon is a dense rainforest that comprises 40% of Brazil’s total area. Not many roads are within it, but those that are, mostly go through either biodiverse forest or grassy hills with sparse trees.

Acre has a unique landscape of small grass hills and sparsely growing trees. The roads often do not cut around the hills like in most of Brazil, but ride the hills instead. A similar landscape can also be seen near Maraba in the state of Pará.

Rural locations in Roraima are mostly open grassy plains with large, distant mountains in the background. Occasionally, you are on roads within the mountains. Furthermore, the grass in Roraima is distinctly thin, and grows in bunches.
The landscape in Rio Grande do Sul can be hilly or flat with lush, green fields. Southern areas can have some resemblance to Uruguay.
Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo often have rolling grassy hills.
Espírito Santo, and the surrounding areas, often have large mountains with exposed rock.

These distinct trees, called Paraná pines, have long horizontal branches with leaves only at the end. They grow mainly in the southern Brazilian states of Paraná, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul.

Coconut palm trees have long leaves, can grow very tall, and have thin trunks. They are common across the north eastern states and sometimes further west or south along the coast.

NOTE: Coconut palms grow across the world and are not unique to Brazil.

Carnaúba palms have short but strong fan-like leaves, and a trunk that is smooth at the top and spiked at the bottom. They are commonly seen in Ceará, Piauí, and Rio Grande de Norte, but are also around the town of Xique Xique in Bahia.
Babassu palms have long, robust leaves comprised of many leaflets. Trunk length can vary from short to tall. They are found throughout the Amazon, or more rarely, down the east coast.

Açai palms produce fruits that are popular globally. Most of these palms are found near Belem, but can be seen across the Amazon. They are distinct in the way the leaflets droop downward along with their unusually thin trunks.

NOTE: Most açai palms are found in the Amazon. However, some visually similar açai subspecies can rarely occur along the east coast from Santa Catarina all the way to Bahia.

Moriche palms have leaves with a rounded fan shape, and often the bottom leaves can be seen dead and drooping down. They are most common in Roraima, Amazonas, Tocantins, Goias, and the Amazonian states, but random clusters can be found quite far away from this region.

NOTE: These palms can additionally be found very commonly in the Amazonian parts of Colombia and Peru.

Macaw palms have thin leaves compared to other palms, and often have a visible spear shaped top. They are very common around Mato Grosso do Sul, northern Tocantins, and around Belo Horizonte, but can be seen much further out sometimes. These palms should be used with caution, and single trees are much less of an indicator than multiple trees.

NOTE: Queen palms can look similar sometimes, but there are less leaves and it looks less dense.

This species of plant, with long stems and many leaves growing up, are very common in Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, and Paraíba. In the dry season, you can still make out the distinct long stems without leaves.
Very tall grass can be often seen in the centre of the country, most notably in the Tocantins, Goiás, Bahia, and Minas Gerais states.

Eucalyptus Grandis, when fully grown, is a very tall tree with plantations all over Brazil. You can find them in both large and very small plantations., as well as randomly growing anywhere. You can see them all over the south, but there are some large plantations in Amapá too.
Sugarcane plantations are by far most common in the state of São Paulo, and are common in Paraná, Mato Grosso do Sul, and in the coastal north eastern states.
Soybeans appear as small, leafy soil grown plants. They are most commonly grown in Mato Grosso, Paraná, and Goiás.
Coffee beans are by far the most common in Minas Gerais, but also can be found in Espírito Santo and northeastern São Paulo.

Alongside ladder poles, round poles can often be found across the south of Brazil, especially São Paulo. These poles are cylindrical and made of concrete.

NOTE: This map and the following wooden pole map was created using statistical analysis of semi-urban and rural locations. 434 locations of 3 poles per location were used across 16 states that were thought to have mixed poles. Regardless of the state, the centre of large cities will often have round poles.
Some states also use wooden poles. They are most commonly seen in Rio Grande do Sul, Roraima, Amazonas, and Rio de Janeiro.

Brazil often uses supports on its electricity poles that connect the crossbar to the stem of the pole. The frequency of pole supports varies greatly state-to-state. It is notably rare in the northeast.

NOTE: This tip only works for poles that have a crossbar.
Poles with a single support are most commonly found in the states of Tocantins, Santa Catarina, and Minas Gerais.

Markings on poles are used by the electricity companies to identify them. This pole ID is long, yellow pole paint with a black code. The ones that start with a letter are found in Bahia and Pernambuco.

Similar to the Bahia and Pernambuco poles, Goiás poles also use long, yellow pole paint with a black paint code, but it always starts with a number. They also have a rarer yellow on black pole ID, which can be either paint or a plate.

This small yellow or orange plate attached onto the pole by thin metal or zip tie is found in Rio Grande do Norte and Pernambuco. This ID is usually much higher up the pole in Pernambuco than in Rio Grande do Norte.
Pole IDs in Paraná are usually made up of black paint and yellow or white painted text.
Most poles in Maranhão have a small beige plate with numbers built into the surface of the pole. This pole ID can be found in Pará and Piauí more rarely.
Utility poles in Paraná on intersections are sometimes painted with the street name. This can sometimes extend to Santa Catarina or Rio Grande do Sul if there are ladder poles in the city.

This poletop, consisting of an asymmetrical crossbar and a support reaching to the middle of the longer part of the crossbar, is the most common poletop in the state of São Paulo. It can also be frequently seen in the states of Rio Grande do Sul, Rio de Janeiro and Mato Grosso do Sul.

This asymmetrical crossbar with no supports is exclusive to Ceara and Rondonia.

NOTE: While the crossbar in Ceara is usually made of concrete, the Rondonian variation features a metal crossbar, and is far less common.
This pole configuration, featuring a zigzag-shaped top bar resting atop a flat crossbar, is exclusive to Ceara and Roraima. The pole is usually much larger than a regular electricity pole.
Poles that have a smooth cone on top, often called a pencil pole, are common in the state of Rio de Janeiro and rarely in Brasília and Manaus.

Gamma-shaped ("Γ") poles containing electricity boxes at the end of the bar are most commonly seen in the state of Rio de Janeiro and in the cities of Belém, Salvador, Fortaleza and Maceió.

NOTE: A variation with a shorter bar is exclusive to Belém.

You may frequently see electricity counters attached to the poles in Cuiabá, Macapá and large cities in the state of Pará.

NOTE: The electricity counter may consist of one or several compartments.
Poles that have one insulator on top and alternating horizontal insulators can be found in Mato Grosso and southern Acre. It is also very rare in Rio Grande do Sul.
Insulators that resemble brown mushrooms are only found in Pernambuco.
Insulators that resemble white mushrooms are found in Bahia and rarely Brasília.
Transparent insulators are mostly in Alagoas in the northeast, and Santa Catarina in the south. They can be seen rarely in Sergipe, Ceará, and Brasília.
These insulators have a shape resembling a spool of thread. They are found mostly in Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo, and have been seen in Ceará.
Insulators in Ceará can sometimes be uniquely long and thin. They are in Goiás too, but are rare.
Poles with horizontal insulators are very common in Pará and less so in Mato Grosso. They are rarely found in Acre, Amapá, Tocantins, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.

Long grey insulators, not including when they are horizontal, are most commonly found in Pará, Mato Grosso, Tocantins, Bahia, Mato Grosso do Sul, Paraná and Santa Catarina.

They are found rarely in Maranhão, Rio Grande do Norte, Alagoas, Sergipe, Rondônia, and Rio Grande do Sul. Other states have between 0 and 5%.
Poles with these black double UFO-shaped insulators in a trident formation are common in Maranhão. The insulator itself is common across many states, but not in this configuration.

These insulators are spherical or cone shaped and suspended on a rod above the insulator bar. They are often referred to as “lollipop” insulators. They are very common in Rio Grande de Norte, Paraíba, Pernambuco, and more rarely, Sergipe.
These dark brown insulators with grey bases are found almost exclusively in Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.
Brazil often uses metal trash baskets outside houses. In Acre and Rondônia, however, it is much more common to see them made of concrete.
Lamps in Minas Gerais and Goias will often feature two parts to them. They can also be found in Rio Grande do Norte, Ceará, Rio Grande do Sul as well as the Federal District.

Lamps in urban northern Paraná sometimes have no lamp arm. Styles contrast, and are either colourful, plastic and industrial, or look fancy and ornate. Both versions are most commonly found in northwest Paraná.

The vast majority of poles in Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Pará, Amapá, Rio Grande do Norte, Pernambuco and Santa Catarina have the lamp arm attached to the pole, as opposed to it being attached with a plate, which is much more common generally.

Lamps in Roraima have a similar style but have different colours in the main cities. Boa Vista, Normandia, and Mucajaí have red lamps, Rorainópolis has blue lamps, Pacaraima and Iracema have green, and Caracaraí has yellow.
Lamps in Ceará often have a fancy and colourful arm, whether as lampposts or attached to utility poles. It sometimes says the town on the arm.
São Paulo has far more divided highways than any other state.
Phone numbers can sometimes be seen underneath kilometre markers in São Paulo.
Cobblestone pavement is most common in the northeast and in Rio Grande do Sul.
Roads with hexagonal concrete tiles can be found across Brazil, but they are more common in Santa Catarina and Minas Gerais.
Some roads in Acre are made of red brick.
Cobblestone roads with randomly sized stones are most common in southeast Rio Grande do Sul and Minas Gerais.

These uneven but mostly square stone roads are seen in western Rio Grande do Sul and west Santa Catarina. The soil will often be very dark in these regions too.

NOTE: The same roads are seen in the Misiones province of Argentina.
You can often see pavements in Rio Grande do Sul that have brown tiles but are either jagged and random, or square. This style can sometimes be seen in Santa Catarina.
Buildings in the southern states, mainly Santa Catarina, can be of European influence (typically vaguely German) in design and style.

Wooden houses on stilts are very common in the state of Acre.

NOTE: They are also seen more rarely in low-lying Amazonas and Pará, as well as various other countries.

Many roads in Piauí have red gravel on the side of the road. The gravel can appear spread above the tarmac shoulder or on roads with curbs.

NOTE: This can appear elsewhere. Use with caution.
In all Generation 4 coverage in Amapá, the front right of the camera is smudged. In addition, all Generation 4 coverage in Amapá features the white car with the blue stripe.
These spheres on top of utility poles are João-de-Barro nests. They are common across the south of Brazil.
The landscape near the town of Uiramuta, in northern Roraima, features a very distinct landscape. It is dry, with large mountains containing numerous “folds.”
Coastal regions in Rio Grande do Sul are recognisable due to being a rare flat wetland, which is uncommon in Brazil.

The 364 through Acre is very recognisable due to the rollercoaster-like landscape and road: the road uniquely rides the hills rather than snaking around them. There is usually no traffic, and is covered mostly by Generation 4 blue car.

The Amazonas 319 has a very lush, bright green and tropical landscape, as it cuts through the Amazon rainforest. The road is flat and mostly unpaved, featuring bright orange soil. However, closer to Manaus the road becomes paved. There are wooden or ladder poles alongside the entire stretch. It is covered by the blue Generation 4 car.

The Pará section of the 163 is often hilly, curvy, dry, and sometimes hazy. It has a wide range of amazonian vegetation. The road is frequently trafficked, usually by transportation trucks. It is covered by the blue Generation 4 car in the north and the Smallcam car in the south.

São Paulo has a square, yellow pole ID paint. It has three letters on top followed by two numbers, a black line, and four more numbers. The three letters represent the municipality within São Paulo, but are rarely visible.
Street signs in Campo Grande and Joinville are stickers wrapped around a pole at intersections. Campo Grande signs usually have extra information and a red and yellow stripe.
Lamps in Rio de Janeiro are curved through the whole of the lamp arm, which is not seen anywhere else.
Teresina lamps are usually blue with an orange arm.
Belém lamp heads are often orange.
Cuiaba lamps are usually a light green, and is one of the few cities that has poles with multiple electricity metres, sometimes 6 to 12.

Lamps in Belo Horizonte and Uberaba in Generation 4 can have a white, numbered plaque attached to the lamp. In Belo Horizonte, the tag starts with 0 or 1, and in Uberaba, it starts with a 1 or 2.

Since this plaque is new, it may appear in other cities in Minas Gerais in the future.
Lamps in Caxias do Sul usually have a zig-zag bent pole and a yellow head.
Poles on Santa Catarina Island (Florianópolis) are painted white with blue and red stripes.
You can often see rifts in Alagoas Generation 3 coverage.

Note: Brazil has many hundreds of trekkers and a couple of unique cars. This section only discusses a couple of prominent and recognizable trekkers and unique cars that sometimes appear in custom maps and the official competitive game modes.
This Amazonian trekker combines boat and walking coverage on and near the Madeira and Aripuana rivers, south of the 319. They are seen travelling through dense rainforest and small villages.

The beautiful National Park of Northeast Maranhão, known for its sand dunes with pools of water, has walking trekker and vehicle coverage. The truck is white with a black bed. The landscape can vary from beach to sandy wetland.

Ilha de Fernando de Noronha is a Brazilian island with official coverage approximately 340 kilometres northeast of Rio Grande do Norte, and the country itself. It is covered by a white buggy, which is visible at the front. The island is similar in vegetation to the closest part of mainland Brazil, and has large exposed rocks. There is also boat coverage around the island.

steps.title: Maps and resources
steps.html:
GeoGuessr’s own official maps are not very good, for a variety of reasons. Plonk It recommends you play these maps instead:

  • A Balanced Brazil (map link) - The main Brazil map. If you are looking to learn and streak Brazil, A Balanced Brazil is used in official Plonk It records, and is recommended to play.
  • Brazil City Streaks (map link) - If you want to practise distinguishing between urban areas.
  • Dirty Brazil (map link) - A map focusing on extremely rural coverage, with mostly dirt roads.

In addition, here are some resources to help you practise Brazil:

  • Plonk It Brazil (map link) - This map contains locations for practising each meta in the Plonk It Brazil guide from step 2 to 3.
  • Brazil Area Codes (map link) - Play this map to practise the various Brazilian area codes.

lm.note: Some roads in Acre are made of red brick.

lm.note: Acre has a unique landscape of small grass hills and sparsely growing trees. The roads often do not cut around the hills like in most of Brazil, but ride the hills instead. A similar landscape can also be seen near Maraba in the state of Pará.

lm.note: Markings on poles are used by the electricity companies to identify them. This pole ID is long, yellow pole paint with a black code. The ones that start with a letter are found in Bahia and Pernambuco.

lm.name: Carnaúba palms
lm.note: Carnaúba palms have short but strong, fan-like leaves and a trunk that is smooth at the top and spiked at the bottom. They are common in Ceará but are also in Piauí and Rio Grande do Norte.

lm.name: Ceará lamps
lm.note: Lamps in Ceará often have a fancy and colourful arm, whether as lampposts or attached to utility poles. It sometimes says the town on the arm.

lm.name: Coffee beans
lm.note: Coffee beans are by far the most common in Minas Gerais, but also can be found in Espírito Santo and northeastern São Paulo.

lm.name: Concrete bins
lm.note: Brazil often uses metal trash baskets outside houses. In Acre and Rondônia, however, it is much more common to see them made of concrete.

lm.name: Espírito Santo - Exposed rock
lm.note: Espírito Santo, and the surrounding areas, often have large mountains with exposed rock.

lm.name: Goiás pole markings
lm.note: Similar to the Bahia and Pernambuco poles, Goiás poles also use long, yellow pole paint with a black paint code, but it always starts with a number. They also have a rarer yellow on black pole ID, which can be either paint or a plate.

lm.name: Ilha de Fernando de Noronha
lm.note: Ilha de Fernando de Noronha is a Brazilian island with official coverage approximately 340 kilometres northeast of Rio Grande do Norte, and the country itself. It is covered by a white buggy, which is visible at the front. The island is similar in vegetation to the closest part of mainland Brazil, and has large exposed rocks. There is also boat coverage around the island.

lm.name: Macaw palms
lm.note: Macaw palms have thin leaves compared to other palms, and often have a visible spear shaped top. They are very common around Mato Grosso do Sul and the surrounding states, but can be seen much further out sometimes. These palms should be used with caution, and single trees are much less of an indicator than multiple trees.

lm.name: Maranhão wide insulators
lm.note: Poles with these wide insulators in a trident formation are common in Maranhão. The insulator itself is common across many states, but not in this configuration.

lm.name: Mato Grosso pole
lm.note: Poles that have one insulator on top and alternating horizontal insulators can be found in Mato Grosso and southern Acre. It is also very rare in Rio Grande do Sul.

lm.name: Paraná pines
lm.note: These distinct trees, called Paraná pines, have long horizontal branches with leaves only at the end. They grow mainly in the southern Brazilian states of Paraná, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul.

lm.name: Paraná pole markings
lm.note: Pole IDs in Paraná are usually made up of black paint and yellow or white painted text.

lm.name: Piauí road
lm.note: Most roads in Piauí have red gravel on the side of the road. Some roads in Generation 4 now have tarmac and kerbs, but some gravel shoulders remain.

lm.name: Rio Grande do Norte and Pernambuco pole plates
lm.note: This small yellow or orange plate attached onto the pole by thin metal or zip tie is found in Rio Grande do Norte and Pernambuco. This ID is usually much higher up the pole in Pernambuco than in Rio Grande do Norte.

lm.name: Rio Grande do Sul pavement
lm.note: You can often see pavements in Rio Grande do Sul that have brown tiles but are either jagged and random, or square. This style can sometimes be seen in Santa Catarina.

lm.name: Rolling grassy hills
lm.note: Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo often have rolling grassy hills.

lm.name: Rural Roraima
lm.note: Rural locations in Roraima are mostly open grassy plains with large, distant mountains in the background. Occasionally, you are on roads within the mountains. Furthermore, the grass in Roraima is distinctly thin, and grows in bunches.

lm.name: Sugarcane plantations
lm.note: Sugarcane plantations are by far most common in the state of São Paulo, and in the coastal north east states, especially Alagoas and Pernambuco.

lm.name: Uneven stone road
lm.note:
These uneven but mostly square stone roads are seen in western Rio Grande do Sul and west Santa Catarina. The soil will often be very dark in these regions too.

NOTE: The same roads are seen in the Misiones province of Argentina.

lm.name: Very tall grass
lm.note: Very tall grass can be often seen in the centre of the country, most notably in the Tocantins, Goiás, Bahia, and Minas Gerais states.

lm.name: Brick Meta - B-Type Brick
lm.note:
The B-type brick can be recognized by its three deep horizontal slots.

It is especially common across northeastern Brazil, including Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, Paraíba, Pernambuco, Sergipe, eastern Piauí, and western Bahia. It is also frequently found in Acre, Manaus, eastern Pará, São Paulo, Mato Grosso do Sul, western Mato Grosso, western Minas Gerais, and Tocantins.

Be careful in transition zones, where both A-type and B-type bricks may appear in the same area.

lm.name: Brick Meta - C-Type Brick
lm.note:
The C-type brick can be recognized by its four deep horizontal slots.

This type is considerably rarer than the A-type and B-type bricks. It is found mainly in southern Bahia, Rio de Janeiro, and some surrounding areas.

Because of its rarity, a clearly visible C-type brick can provide strong regional information, although other clues should still be considered.

lm.name: Brick Meta - D-Type Brick
lm.note:
The D-type brick has very fine cracks, shallow slots, or slight horizontal ridges. From a distance, these markings may look like faint lines, and some bricks may appear almost completely smooth.

Unlike the other types, D-type bricks can be found throughout Brazil. They are especially common in large cities and in areas such as Belém, central Minas Gerais, central Goiás, São Paulo, and the eastern coast between João Pessoa and Rio de Janeiro.

Since D-type bricks can coexist with other brick types, prioritize a clearly identifiable A-type or B-type brick when both are present.

lm.name: Brick Meta - E-Type Brick
lm.note:
The E-type brick has multiple deep horizontal slots, usually six or more.

It may resemble some versions of the D-type brick, but its slots are generally deeper, clearer, and less numerous than the extremely fine ridges found on D-type bricks.

This type is uncommon but regionally useful, as it is mainly associated with central Bahia, northern Alagoas, and northern Sergipe. Only use this clue when the slots are clearly visible.

lm.name: Brick Meta - Single-Line Brick
lm.note:
The single-line brick can be recognized by its single visible horizontal slot or groove.

This brick is not a useful regional clue. It is widespread across Brazil and does not follow a consistent geographic pattern.

Treat it as non-diagnostic: do not use it to determine the state or region. Prioritize clearly identifiable A-type, B-type, C-type, D-type, or E-type bricks and other surrounding clues instead.

This type is included as a negative clue: seeing it should not influence your regional guess.

lm.name: Brick Meta: A-Type
lm.note:
The A-type brick can be recognized by its two deep horizontal slots.

It is the dominant brick type across southern Brazil, especially in Paraná, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul. It is also common in Rondônia, Roraima, Amapá, western Pará, Maranhão, western Piauí, southern Bahia, Tocantins, and parts of Goiás.

Some exceptions and transition zones exist, particularly where A-type and B-type bricks overlap.

lm.name: Brazil
lm.note: Licence plates in Brazil were white until 2018. Now, a white plate with a blue stripe on top is used. Red is still used for commercial vehicles.

lm.name: Agriculture - Coffee
lm.note: Coffee beans are by far the most common in Minas Gerais, but also can be found in Espirito Santo and northeastern Sao Paulo.

lm.name: Agriculture - Cotton
lm.note: 73% of Cotton Production in Brazil takes place in Mato Grosso. 20% take place in the western border of Bahia. Other minor spots are western Minas Gerais, Southern Goias and Northern MGDS

lm.name: Agriculture - Eucalyptus Grandis
lm.note: Eucalyptus Grandis, when fully grown, is a very tall tree with plantations all over Brazil. You can find them in both large and very small plantations, as well as randomly growing anywhere. You can see them all over the south, but there are some large plantations in Amapa too.

lm.name: Agriculture - Soybeans
lm.note: Soybeans appear as small, leafy soil grown plants. They are most commonly grown in Mato Grosso, Paraná, and Goiás.

lm.name: Agriculture - Sugarcane
lm.note: Sugarcane plantations are by far most common in the state of Sao Paulo, and in the coastal north east states, especially Alagoas and Pernambuco.

lm.name: Architecture - European Architecture
lm.note: Buildings in the southern states, mainly Santa Catarina, can be of European influence (typically vaguely German) in design and style.

lm.name: Architecture - Red Brick Architecture
lm.note: Houses made out of red brick are more common in Northeastern Brazil.

lm.name: Architecture - Stilt Houses
lm.note: Wooden houses on stilts are very common in the state of Acre.

lm.name: Car Meta - Noronha Car Meta
lm.note: Ilha de Fernando de Noronha is covered by a white buggy which sometimes has a visible front.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Amapa Blur
lm.note: In all Generation 4 coverage in Amapá, the front right of the camera is smudged. In addition, all Generation 4 coverage in Amapá features the white car with the blue stripe.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - BR-156 in Northern Amapa
lm.note: This road is characterized by the Amapa Blur (slight blur at the front of a blue-striped car), the red, and the road angle to Northwest. There are frequently Areca palms growing near this road.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Camera Glitch
lm.note: Northwest Rio Grande do Sul has coverage with this camera glitch in Generation 3.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - East-West BR156 in Amapa
lm.note: This part of the BR156 can be recognized by the Amapa Blur (slight blur at the front right of the blue-striped car). It's the only Amapa Blur coverage on a road that goes East-West. This part of the road is paved.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Flooded Coverage
lm.note: Flooded coverage can be found between Macau and Macauzinho in Rio Grande do Norte.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Hazy Sky
lm.note: Hazy Sky Coverage is very common in Porto Velho.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Post Bushfire Coverage
lm.note: The road between Caico, RGDN and Santa Luzia, Paraiba is unique with its post bushfire coverage. The part in Paraiba often has outer dashed lines

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Rifts

lm.name: Infrastructure - 2 Ridge Insulator
lm.note: Memorize the distribution map.

lm.name: Infrastructure - 3 Ridge Insulator
lm.note:
Most commonly found in Paraiba in the North, and in Parana, Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro. It's pretty rare.

Memorize the distribution map for more details.

Note by MB: They're also different to the lollipop insulator, where the ridges have different sizes.

lm.name: Infrastructure - 4 Ridge Insulator
lm.note:
Widespread, but can still resolve some 50/50s. Memorize the map.

Also, in Sao Paulo, it's common in Sao Paulo city, and uncommon outside of it.

lm.name: Infrastructure - 5 Ridges Insulator
lm.note: Insulators with 5 ridges are very common in Sao Paulo.

lm.name: Infrastructure - 90° Crossbar
lm.note: Right angle top bars are common in Brasília

lm.name: Infrastructure - Aerodynamic Lamp
lm.note: Aerodynamic Lamp Heads are common in Fortaleza.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Alagoas Lamp
lm.note: Different colors possible

lm.name: Infrastructure - Aracaju Lamp Arm ID
lm.note: Unique ID on a common lamp head. Sometimes, you can't see much of the code, only zip ties.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Aracaju Road Sign
lm.note: Aracaju, Sergipe

lm.name: Infrastructure - Barra Do Garcas Lamp Arm
lm.note: Barra Do Garcas, Mato Grosso (border to Goias)

lm.name: Infrastructure - Belem ID
lm.note: Lots of rare pole IDs in the city

lm.name: Infrastructure - Belo Horizonte Lamp
lm.note: Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais

lm.name: Infrastructure - Bend Attached to Pole
lm.note: The vast majority of poles in Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Pará, Amapá, Rio Grande do Norte, Pernambuco and Santa Catarina have the lamp arm attached to the pole, as opposed to it being attached with a plate, which is much more common generally.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Big Electricity Counter on Pole
lm.note:
Big electricity counters on the pole are most common in Mato Grosso, Para and Amapa.

Unlike their smaller version, they do not appear in Paraiba.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Black&Yellow Bollards
lm.note: Black & Yellow bollards of different kinds are common in Salvador.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Blue ID
lm.note: Unique to Rio Branco

lm.name: Infrastructure - Blue Lamp Arm ID
lm.note: Small, blue, hanging from the lamp arm. Found in Cuiaba (bend attached to pole), and in the cities of Riberao Preto and Sao Paulo (normal lamp arm)

lm.name: Infrastructure - Boa Vista ID
lm.note: Boa Vista, Roraima

lm.name: Infrastructure - BR-101 in the Northeast
lm.note:
This road is divided. What makes it special is that one direction as asphalt and the other direction has concrete pavement.

This does not apply to the entire road anymore

lm.name: Infrastructure - Brasilia Streetsign
lm.note: Brasilia, Distrito Federal

lm.name: Infrastructure - Brown Mushroom Insulator
lm.note: Pernambuco sometimes uses these brown mushroom insulators.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Campinas Sidewalk
lm.note: The city of Campinas, SP is known for it's unique and artistic patterns of black and white stones on its sidewalks.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Cascavel Black Number Arrow
lm.note: A tiny black pole paint, containing a white number with a triangle-shaped arrow. Unique to Cascavel, Parana.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Cascavel Blue Lamp
lm.note: The town of Cascavel, Paraná uses this blue lamp. However, in newer coverage it is very rare to find.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Ceara Lamp Arms
lm.note: Lamps in Ceará often have a fancy and colourful arm, whether as lampposts or attached to utility poles. It sometimes says the town on the arm.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Ceara Poletop
lm.note: This assymetrical pole with no supports appears statewide in Ceara and sometimes Rondonia. (The Sao Paulo pole has a support bar)

lm.name: Infrastructure - Center White Lines
lm.note: White Center lines are very common in Joao Pessoa. Yellow dashed lines are rare.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Chessboard Sidewalk
lm.note: The sidewalks with a chessboard pattern are common in Curitiba, PR.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Cobblestone Pavement
lm.note: Cobblestone pavement is most common in the northeast and in Rio Grande do Sul.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Colorful Signpost
lm.note: These colorful, thick signposts can be found in different cities in the state of Sao Paulo.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Compact Electricity Counter on Pole
lm.note:
An electricity counter with a compact design can be seen in Mato Grosso, Para, Amapa and Paraiba.

The "less compact" variant with several counters does not exist in Paraiba.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Concrete Trash Bins
lm.note: Brazil often uses metal trash baskets outside houses. In Acre and Rondônia, however, it is much more common to see them made of concrete.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Connector in Bend
lm.note: Meta for Sao Paulo. Only counts when the connector is pointing downwards. The connectors pointing upwards are generic.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Corroded Streetsign
lm.note: All the street signs in Palmas are corroded.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Crossbar with no support
lm.note: Crossbars with no support bars are almost exclusively found in Piaui, Ceara, Rio Grande do Norte and Alagoas. They also frequently appear in the North-East in general, and in Rondonia and Roraima.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Curitiba Sidewalk
lm.note: The two most typical sidewalk patterns in Curitiba, PR.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Dark Brown Insulator on Grey Base
lm.note: These dark brown insulators with grey bases are found almost exclusively in Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Divided Highway
lm.note: São Paulo has far more divided highways than any other state.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Embedded Pole ID
lm.note: Yellow plate embedded into pole. Mainly in Maranhao, spill into Para and Piaui.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Exremely Long Insulator
lm.note:
This one is basically a sub-category of the 6+ Ridge Insulator. It's common in Para, Parana, Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul.

However, it's not always easy to tell apart, but the longer the insulator feels, the more you should consider those states.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Fancy Lamp - Campo Mourão
lm.note: "Fancy Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Campo Mourão.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Fancy Lamp - Cidade Gaucha
lm.note: "Fancy Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Cidade Gaucha. Notably, it's very similar to the one from Campo Mourao.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Fancy Lamp - Goioere
lm.note: "Fancy Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one - with the yellow support - is unique to the town of Goioere. However, in newer coverage, the yellow supports are rarer to find.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Fancy Lamp - Loanda
lm.note: "Fancy Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one - with a plain white lamp and no painted patterns on it - is unique to the town of Loanda.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Fancy Lamp - Umuarama
lm.note: "Fancy Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Umuarama. It is strikingly similar to the lamp from Cidade Gaucha.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Fancy Lamp - Umuarama
lm.note: "Fancy Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific, uniquely shaped one is unique to the town of Umuarama.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Florianopolis Pole
lm.note: Poles on Florianopolis, especially on Santa Catarina Island are painted white with blue and red stripes.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Florianopolis Sign
lm.note: Sometimes also with a white line instead of a red line.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Fortaleza ID
lm.note: These two types of IDs are common in Fortaleza (two pictures)

lm.name: Infrastructure - Gamma + Box
lm.note:
Gamma pole with an electricity box at the end of the crossbeam. Most common in Belem, Salvador and Rio de Janeiro. Can appear occasionally in Ceara and Alagoas.

In RJ, they are particularly common in Sao Goncalo, but appear statewide.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Goias Pole ID
lm.note: The Goias pole ID uses yellow paint with black numbers or a black plate with yellow numbers. Unlike the Bahia and Pernambuco IDs, the ID consists exclusively of digits.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Grass Verge
lm.note: Grass verges between the sidewalk and the road are common in Curitiba.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Green Lamp
lm.note: There are three large cities with green lamps: Cuiaba, Manaus and Vitoria

lm.name: Infrastructure - Hexagonal Pavement
lm.note: Roads with hexagonal concrete tiles can be found across Brazil, but they are more common in Santa Catarina and Minas Gerais.

lm.name: Infrastructure - High attached ID
lm.note: Yellow plate attached by zip tie or metal strip. If it is higher up on the pole, it's in Pernambuco.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Holey Ladder Pole
lm.note: Ladder Poles with holes in them are very common in Joao Pessoa (but not unique)

lm.name: Infrastructure - Horizontal Insulators
lm.note: Poles with horizontal insulators are very common in Pará and less so in Mato Grosso. They are rarely found in Acre, Amapá, Tocantins, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Horizontal Insulators with Top
lm.note: Poles that have one insulator on top and alternating horizontal insulators can be found in Mato Grosso and southern Acre. It is also very rare in Rio Grande do Sul.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Huge Electric Box on Pole
lm.note: Electric meter boxes can be seen in other cities, but in Cuiaba, there are usually 3-6 or even more on one pole.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Huge pole ID
lm.note: This rather large pole ID is common in Betim, Minas Gerais.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Imperatriz holey ID
lm.note: This city ID is distinct thanks to the holes on the sides.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Imperatriz Ornate Lamp
lm.note: Imperatriz, Maranhao

lm.name: Infrastructure - Internet Poster
lm.note: Internet Advertisements attached to poles are very common in Natal. Mnemonic: Internatal :)

lm.name: Infrastructure - Ipiranga Lamp
lm.note: These red lamps that resemble Belém lamps can be found in the neighborhood of Ipiranga in Florianopolis.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Irregular Cobblestone
lm.note: Cobblestone roads with randomly sized stones are most common in southeast Rio Grande do Sul and Minas Gerais.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Itumbiara Red Lamp
lm.note: Itumbiara, Goias

lm.name: Infrastructure - Joao de Barro nests
lm.note: These spheres on top of utility poles are João-de-Barro nests. They are common across the south of Brazil.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Joao Pessoa Stone Pavement
lm.note: Distinct stone sidewalks & driveways in Joao Pessoa.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Joinville Lamp
lm.note: Joinville, Santa Catarina

lm.name: Infrastructure - Joinville Street Sign
lm.note: Not to be confused with the Curitiba sign, which can also be attached to a pole.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Kilometer Marker with Phone Number
lm.note: Phone numbers can sometimes be seen underneath kilometre markers in São Paulo.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Lack of Poles
lm.note: Suspicious lack of poles, and curved lamp posts in their place, are indicative of Brasília.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Little Guy Lamp
lm.note: This cute lamp is unique to Gurupi.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Lollipop Insulators
lm.note: These insulators are spherical or cone shaped and suspended on a rod above the insulator bar. They are often referred to as “lollipop” insulators. They are very common in Rio Grande de Norte, Paraíba, Pernambuco, and more rarely, Sergipe.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Londrina Black Pole ID
lm.note: These black pole IDs are common in the state of Paraná, except for the capital Curitiba. If the black pole has a decimal marker (.) in the number, it's in Londrina.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Londrina Blue Number on Pole
lm.note: The town of Londrina, Paraná sometimes has little blue numbers painted on its poles.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Low Attached ID
lm.note: Yellow plate attached by zip tie or metal strip. If it is lower on the pole, it is RGDN.

lm.name: Infrastructure - MA006
lm.note: Most of this road has a thick (1m) stripe of red dirt on the sides of the road. The road is oriented North-South and frequently shows Babassu palms

lm.name: Infrastructure - Macapa Lamp
lm.note: Macapa, Amapa

lm.name: Infrastructure - Macapa Pole ID
lm.note: Macapa, Amapa

lm.name: Infrastructure - Maceio ID
lm.note: These two IDs are rare but unique to Maceio.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Maceio Lamp
lm.note: Long posts with top arm bend and yellow or grey top dot at the bottom.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Maceio Streetsign
lm.note: Also available in blue.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Manaus Pole ID
lm.note: Pole IDs in Manaus are usually above the lamp attachment.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Maraba Skull Box
lm.note: Yellow skull stickers are common on electric boxes in Maraba.

lm.name: Infrastructure - MGDS Flag
lm.note: In urban settings, state flags might show up. Might pay off sometimes.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Minas Gerais ID with 0/1
lm.note: These pole IDs are specific for Minas Gerais. If they start with 0 or 1, it's Belo Horizonte.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Natal ID
lm.note: Natal, Rio Grande do Norte

lm.name: Infrastructure - Neon-Yellow Horizontal ID
lm.note: Neon-yellow horizontal IDs are specific to Sao Paulo. Do not confuse with Campo Grande or Vitoria (they have vertical, and smaller, neon-yellow IDs)

lm.name: Infrastructure - Neon-Yellow Pole ID
lm.note: Neon-yellow, vertical IDs can be found in Campo Grande, MS and Vitoria, ES. Do not confuse with horizontal neon-yellow IDs (Sao Paulo)

lm.name: Infrastructure - Onitel Sticker
lm.note: Unique to Luziania, GO

lm.name: Infrastructure - Open Electric Box
lm.note: Open or trashed electric boxes appear frequently in Maraba and Santarém (both Para).

lm.name: Infrastructure - Orange Lamp
lm.note: Orange Lamps are common in Belem.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Orange Lamp Arm
lm.note: Very common in Teresina, one of the most well-known urban Brazil metas.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Outer Dashed Lines
lm.note: Outer Dashed Lines can rarely be found in Rio Grande do Norte or other northeast states.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Para specific Pole ID
lm.note: Pare uses these state-wide pole IDs.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Paraiba ID
lm.note: This ID is uncommon, but unique to Paraiba (most common in the capital Joao Pessoa).

lm.name: Infrastructure - Paraiba Lamp
lm.note: The shape matters.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Parana Black Paint Pole ID
lm.note: Pole IDs in Paraná are usually made up of black paint and yellow or white painted text. They do not appear in the capital of Paraná: Curitiba.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Parana Black Square
lm.note: This tiny black paint is rarely found on larger poles in Paraná. Still worth a quick scan, especially in urban locs.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Parana Road Pole Paint
lm.note: Utility poles in Paraná on intersections are sometimes painted with the street name. This is because metal signs are expensive. This is also possible on Northern Rio Grande do Sul ladder poles. An exception is the town of Sinop, Mato Grosso.

lm.name: Infrastructure - PARE on stone
lm.note: Stone road markings are unique to Caxias do Sul, RS.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Pencil Pole Top
lm.note: This little hat on the top, which makes the whole pole resemble a pencil, is most common in Rio de Janeiro, but can also be found in Manaus and Distrito Federal.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Piles of Dirt Meta
lm.note: Common in Boa Vista

lm.name: Infrastructure - Pole Company
lm.note: Electricity company names in Brazil are commonly engraved onto the poles, with their names sometimes corresponding to state names. For example, CELPA stands for Para, COSERN for Rio Grande do Norte or COELCE for Ceara.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Pole Paint starting with letter
lm.note: Yellow paint with black numbers, starts with a letter. Possible in Bahia and Pernambuco. The letter is often specific to a town. Goias uses similar paint IDs, but they consist only of digits.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Pole-Attached Sign
lm.note: Some poles in Curitiba, PR have street signs attached to them. Curitiba still uses regular, generic street signs, though.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Pole-Wrapped Sign
lm.note: These blue pole-wrapped signs are unique to Campo Grande.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Porto Alegre ID
lm.note: Porto Alegre, Rio Grande do Sul

lm.name: Infrastructure - Porto Velho Pole ID
lm.note: Porto Velho, Rondonia

lm.name: Infrastructure - Recife Lamp
lm.note: Recife, Pernambuco

lm.name: Infrastructure - Rectangle on Pole Arm
lm.note: Unique for Recife. Can be faded or even have different colors. It's the shape that matters.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Red Brick Pavement
lm.note: Some roads in Acre are made of red brick.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Red Gravel
lm.note: Most roads in Piauí have red gravel on the side of the road. Some roads in Generation 4 now have tarmac and kerbs, but some gravel shoulders remain.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Red Sticker on Lamp
lm.note: This red sticker below the lamp is unique to Fortaleza.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Rio de Janeiro Lamp
lm.note: Curvy lamp arm, usually big head.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Rio de Janeiro Landbridge
lm.note: This map west of the city of Rio de Janeiro is unique due to the water in the south, the roadlines (double yellow - double broken yellow - single broken white) and the little wall in the North. Rio mountains can be seen in most sections of the road to the North.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Rio De Janeiro Polepaint
lm.note: This yellow polepaint, similar to Sao Paulo, but with all numbers, can be found in Rio de Janeiro.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Rio de Janeiro Taxi
lm.note: Taxis in Rio de Janeiro are completely yellow.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Rio Weird Pole
lm.note: When there is something out of the ordinary happening with the pole, it's Rio de Janeiro.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Roraima Lamps
lm.note: Lamps in Roraima have a similar style but have different colours in the main cities. Boa Vista, Normandia, and Mucajaí have red lamps, Rorainópolis has blue lamps, Pacaraima and Iracema have green, and Caracaraí has yellow.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Round Pole
lm.note: Alongside ladder poles, round poles can often be found across the south of Brazil, especially São Paulo. These poles are cylindrical and made of concrete.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Salvador Lamp Arm ID
lm.note: Long yellow ID on the lamp arm, can be very hard to spot.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Salvador Sidewalk
lm.note: Unique sidewalk, can have other black and white broken tile patterns.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Santarem Lamp
lm.note: Santarem, Para

lm.name: Infrastructure - Sao Luis ID
lm.note: This rare ID is specific to Sao Luis. However, the embedded Maranhao IDs are more common.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Sao Luis Pointy Lamp
lm.note: Pointy front of lamp head, blue or yellow top light.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Sao Paulo Lamp
lm.note: Straight long lamp neck, with tight top bend, usually thin head.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Sao Paulo Pole
lm.note:
Assymetrical crossbeam and insulator position with a long support bar reaching to the middle of the longer part of the crossbeam.

Extremely common in Sao Paulo, common in Rio Grande do Sul. Less common Rio de Janeiro, Espirito Santo and Mato Grosso do Sul (where it appears most oftenly in Tres Lagoas). Rare in Mato Grosso.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Sao Paulo Polepaint
lm.note: Sao Paulo Metropolitan Area has these yellow pole paints with a three letter code. The letters stand for the town. SPU is the most important code, standing for the main city.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Serra dos Orgaos
lm.note: This road can be found North of Rio de Janeiro (city). It is a concrete road with black tar behind the road lines.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Short Gamma + Box
lm.note: Short crossbeam, support bar and electricity box at the end of the crossbeam. Only found in Belem. (unlike the regular Gamma pole with box which can also be found in Salvador and Rio de Janeiro).

lm.name: Infrastructure - Small Red Tactile Pavement
lm.note: Small tile, circular bumps, red tactile pavement is very common in Vitoria, ES. (Do not confuse with Florianopolis, which has large tile red tactile pavement).

lm.name: Infrastructure - Southern Sidewalk
lm.note: You can often see pavements in Rio Grande do Sul that have brown tiles but are either jagged and random, or square. This style can sometimes be seen in Santa Catarina.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Speedbumps
lm.note: Yellow dashed lines and speedbumps are very common in Brasília. (but not unique)

lm.name: Infrastructure - Spool Insulators
lm.note: These insulators have a shape resembling a spool of thread. They are found mostly in Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo, and have been seen in Ceará.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Square Paint ID
lm.note: This ID with two sections, the upper one being a square with a number in it, appears in Pernambuco.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Striped Curbs
lm.note: Black and white striped curbs are common in Boa Vista.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Surprising Wooden Pole
lm.note: In Porto Alegre, there is noticeably more foliage, cleaner, and more spacious than any other city which makes the common wooden poles look somewhat out of place.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Teresina ID
lm.note: Long & Horizontal ID

lm.name: Infrastructure - Thick Bottom Insulator
lm.note:
They're found almost anywhere, but can still resolve some 50/50s:

They are only rarely found in Rio Grande do Norte.

Also they're less common in Pernambuco, Parana, Santa Catarina.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Thin Long Insulator
lm.note: Insulators in Ceará can sometimes be uniquely long and thin. They are in Goiás too, but are rare.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Thin Red Stripe
lm.note: A road with a thin, red stripe out of gravel can be found east of Teresina, Piaui.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Tiny Lamp - Araruna
lm.note: "Tiny Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Araruna.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Tiny Lamp - Cianorte
lm.note: "Tiny Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Cianorte.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Tiny Lamp - Cruzeiro do Oeste
lm.note: "Tiny Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Cruzeiro do Oeste.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Tiny Lamp - Loanda
lm.note: "Tiny Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Loanda.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Tiny Lamp - Maringa
lm.note: "Tiny Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Maringa.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Tiny Lamp - Paranavai
lm.note: "Tiny Lamps" are unique to Northwest-Paraná. This specific one is unique to the town of Paranavai.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Tocantins specific lamp
lm.note: This lamp with a short arm and top light is specific to Tocantins.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Tocantins specific lamp
lm.note: This blue lamp with top light and the unique pattern on the underside is specific to Tocantins.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Tocantins specific lamp
lm.note: This long blue lamp with a top light and a unique pattern on the underside is specific to Tocantins.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Transparent Mushroom Insulator
lm.note: Transparent, mushroom-shaped insulators are common in Alagoas. They less frequently appear in Coastal Santa Catarina. Rarely, they also appear in coastal Rio Grande do Sul, coastal Sao Paulo and in Sergipe.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Trident Pole
lm.note: Poles with these wide insulators in a trident formation are common in Maranhão. The insulator itself is common across many states, but not in this configuration.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Two Part Lamp - Goias Variant
lm.note:
2-part lamp, most commonly seen in Minas Gerais and Goias. This particular variant with a the pole visible underneath is more common in Goias.

Otherwise, this pole appears in Rio Grande do Norte and Rio Grande do Sul (very useful if you have North/South vibe), spill in Distrito Federal and extremely rarely in Para, Mato Grosso and Rondonia.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Two Part Lamp - Minas Gerais Variant
lm.note:
2-part lamp, most commonly seen in Minas Gerais and Goias. This particular variant - with both parts enveloping the lamp - is more common in Minas Gerais.

Otherwise, this pole appears in Rio Grande do Norte and Rio Grande do Sul (very useful if you have North/South vibe), spill in Distrito Federal and extremely rarely in Para, Mato Grosso and Rondonia.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Uberaba ID
lm.note: In Uberaba, pole IDs start with 2 or 3, and sometimes with 1. In Belo Horizonte, meanwhile, they start with 0 or 1. They do not appear in any other cities in MG.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Uneven Stone Pavement
lm.note: These uneven but mostly square stone roads are seen in western Rio Grande do Sul and west Santa Catarina. The soil will often be very dark in these regions too.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Vitoria Electric Boxes
lm.note: Metal electricity box, sandwiched between plastic electricity boxes are very common in Vitoria, ES.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Vitoria ID
lm.note: Red pole ID.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Vitoria Streetsign
lm.note: Unique streetsign design in Vitoria.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Weird Road Layout
lm.note: Roundabouts and weird layout roads that are mostly empty, and perfectly flat, are common in Palmas.

lm.name: Infrastructure - White Mushroom Insulator
lm.note: Bahia uses these unique white insulators sometimes.

lm.name: Infrastructure - WiFi-Password Pole-ID
lm.note: If you find pole IDs with codes that resemble WiFi-passwords (mix of digits, upper- and lowercase letters), you're in Curitiba, PR.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Wooden Pole
lm.note: Some states also use wooden poles. They are most commonly seen in Rio Grande do Sul, Roraima, Amazonas, and Rio de Janeiro.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Yellow Outer Lines
lm.note: Yellow outer lines on urban roads are very common in Curitiba.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Yellow Stick
lm.note: This yellow stick is common in Rio Branco, and often has a sign attached to it.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Zig-Zag lamp arm
lm.note: In Brazil, this Zig-Zag lamp arm is unique to Caxias do Sul.

lm.name: Infrastructure - ZigZag-Topbar
lm.note: This pole configuration, featuring a zigzag-shaped top bar resting atop a flat crossbar, is exclusive to Ceara and Roraima. The pole is usually much larger than a regular electricity pole.

lm.name: Infrastructure -6+ Ridge Insulators
lm.note:
These insulators have six or more ridges.

Commonly found in:

  • Bahia, Tocantins, Maranhao
  • Para, Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul
  • Parana Santa Catarina

Uncommon in:

  • Acre, Rondonia, Amapa
  • Piaui, Goias, Sao Paulo, RGDS

Rarely in:

  • RGDN, Rio de Janeiro

lm.name: Landscape - Acre Landscape
lm.note: Acre has a unique landscape of small grass hills and sparsely growing trees. The roads often do not cut around the hills like in most of Brazil, but ride the hills instead. A similar landscape can also be seen near Maraba in the state of Pará.

lm.name: Landscape - Amazon Rainforest
lm.note: The Amazon is a dense rainforest that compromises 40% of Brazil's total area. Not many roads are within it, but those that are, mostly go through either biodiverse forest or grassy hills with sparse trees.

lm.name: Landscape - Amazonas 319
lm.note: The Amazonas 319 has a very lush, bright green and tropical landscape, as it cuts through the Amazon rainforest. The road is flat and mostly unpaved, featuring bright orange soil. However, closer to Manaus the road becomes paved. There are wooden or ladder poles alongside the entire stretch. It is covered by the blue Generation 4 car.

lm.name: Landscape - BR-163 in Para
lm.note: The Pará section of the 163 is often hilly, curvy, dry, and sometimes hazy. It has a wide range of amazonian vegetation. The road is frequently trafficked, usually by transportation trucks. It is covered by the blue Generation 4 car.

lm.name: Landscape - BR174 in Amazonas
lm.note: This road can be recognized by the Amazonian looking trees and the NW/SE angle. It always has Gen 4 and an exposed, blue car front.

lm.name: Landscape - BR230 in Amazonas

lm.name: Trekker - Noronha Boat Trekker

lm.name: Vegetation - Acai Palm
lm.note:
Açai palms produce fruits that are popular globally. Most of these palms are found near Belem, but can be seen across the Amazon. They are distinct in the way the leaflets droop downward along with their unusually thin trunks.

Note by MB: They are very similar to the Jucara Palm (which grows in Southern Brazil). Tips for differentiation:

  • Acai Palms have more thick, robust leaves (comparatively)
  • Acai Palms like growing in bunches

lm.name: Vegetation - Acrocomia Totai (Paraguay Palm)
lm.note:
This palm is commonly mistaken to be a Macaw Palm (Acrocomia Aculeata). The key difference is that the trunk of the "Paraguay Palm" is often smoother and less irregular. The crown can also give some hints although it's difficult to catch the differences

  • Macaw Palm: More open and irregular, with leaves spreading in different directions.
  • "Paraguay Palm": Denser and more compact, sometimes looking neater and rounder.

The distribution is also a bit different, as this palm usually is closer to Paraguay than the Macaw Palm which stretches further.

lm.name: Vegetation - Babassu Palm
lm.note: Babassu palms have long, robust leaves comprised of many leaflets. Trunk length can vary from short to tall. They are found throughout the Amazon, or more rarely, down the east coast.

lm.name: Vegetation - Carnauba Palm
lm.note: Carnaúba palms have short but strong, fan-like leaves and a trunk that is smooth at the top and spiked at the bottom. They are common in Ceará but are also in Piauí and Rio Grande do Norte.

lm.name: Vegetation - Coconut Palm
lm.note: Coconut palm trees have long leaves, can grow very tall, and have thin trunks. They are common across the north eastern states and sometimes further west or south along the coast.

lm.name: Vegetation - Jucara Palm
lm.note:
Closely related to the Açaí palm, they are really hard to distinguish apart from each other. However, the Açaí palm grows mostly in the northern flat regions of Brazil, while the Juçara grows in the mountainous south-east regions of Brazil anywhere from Espirito Santo down to Rio Grande do Sul.

Here some tips for differences:

  • The leaves of Jucara Palms are thinner
  • Jucara Palms have more space, they don't like growing close to each other.

lm.name: Vegetation - Macaw Palm
lm.note: Macaw palms, often called Paraguay palms, have thin leaves compared to other palms, and often have a visible spear shaped top. They are very common around Mato Grosso do Sul and the surrounding states, but can be seen much further out sometimes. These palms should be used with caution, and single trees are much less of an indicator than multiple trees.

lm.name: Vegetation - Moriche Palm
lm.note: Moriche palms have leaves with a rounded fan shape. They are most common in Amazonas, Acre, and Roraima, but can be found in all of the Amazonian states.

lm.name: Vegetation - Mysterious Northeastern Plant
lm.note: This species of plant, with long stems and many leaves growing up, are very common in Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, and Paraíba. In the dry season, you can still make out the distinct long stems without leaves.

lm.name: Vegetation - Parana Pine
lm.note: These distinct trees, called Paraná pines, have long horizontal branches with leaves only at the end. They grow mainly in the southern Brazilian states of Paraná, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul.

lm.name: Vegetation - Pine Trees
lm.note: Pine Trees are common in Southern Brazil, but are rarely ever found north of Belo Horizonte.

lm.name: Vegetation - Queen Palm
lm.note:
Queen palms have leaf stems that point upwards on the trunk and then "bow down" again to the ground due to gravity. They are native to South America. In Brazil, they are mainly found along the coast between Rio de Janeiro and Porto Alegre.

Outside of South America, they're also found in Florida and East Coast Queensland.

lm.name: Vegetation - Tocantins Grass
lm.note: Very tall grass can be often seen in the centre of the country, most notably in the Tocantins, Goiás, Bahia, and Minas Gerais states.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner
lm.name: Pole
lm.note:
The most common poles in Brazil resemble a ladder at the bottom. They are rectangular, with long segments at the base and small holes near the top. Chilean poles look similar but have 1–2 larger sections at the bottom instead of 3+ like Brazilian poles.

You might also find rounded concrete or wooden poles in Brazil, but they are less common and can be used for region-guessing within the country.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta Latin America - Beginner
lm.name: Road marker
lm.note:
A blue road marker with the road number at the top and the kilometer at the bottom is common in Brazil. Sometimes, the first two letters of the road number can tell you the state you're in (unless it starts with "BR").

(If you zoom out on the map where you can guess and look at Brazil, you’ll see short two-letter abbreviations for Brazilian states.)

lm.name: Amapá blur
lm.note: Gen 4 coverage in the state of Amapá has a distinct blur in the front right of the panorama. Make sure you have the striped car.

lm.name: Brown mushroom insulator
lm.note: Brown mushroom insulators appear in (mostly urban) Pernambuco.

lm.name: East of Belo QR Code
lm.note: A small region just east of Belo Horizonte has a little QR code sticker on almost every pole that's found nowhere else in the country.

lm.name: Lollipop insulator
lm.note: In the states of Rio Grande do Norte, Paraíba and Pernambuco, these two types of insulators on thin stems can be found. One looks like a thick cone that gets thinner toward the bottom, and the other has a sort of rounded silhouette - careful, it's easy to confuse with another insulator that can also be found elsewhere, with three equal width ridges. The bottom ridge has to be substantially smaller in order to create the round shape.

lm.name: Maranhao black and white pickup
lm.note: In northern Maranhao, Google used a recognizable pickup truck with a white cab and a black bed for some footage around Lencois Maranhenses National Park

lm.name: Paraná black dot
lm.note: If you see a little square black dot low on the flat side of a ladder pole, you're going to be in Paraná. Other states may have unpainted square indents, some white or silver dots/stickers, but only in Paraná is it ever black. Its absence does not mean you are not in Paraná, and it appears to be a relatively new practice (found mostly on newer poles).

lm.name: UFO Trident
lm.note: In rural Maranhao, you will often see trident poles with large, UFO-like insulators. These insulators are common elsewhere as well, but with the trident config it's going to be Maranhao.

lm.name: White mushroom insulator
lm.note: The white mushroom insulators are typical for Bahia, but I also found some on the southern border of Pernambuco. They are generally more common in urban areas than in rural ones.

lm.name: Brazil
lm.note:
Area codes are common to see in Brazil. They are often notated using parentheses, or at minimum as two separate numbers. Phone numbers are sometimes without area codes, and without them will be 8 numbers long for landline and 9 for mobile.

The pattern for each of the states is very learnable and useful. The area codes are grouped by first digit, so even just learning those can already help a lot. Notably, area codes ending in 1 will always be around major cities and state capitals.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Flooded Coverage

lm.name: Infrastructure - Divided Highway
