lm.name: Infrastructure - MA006
lm.note: Most of this road has a thick (1m) stripe of red dirt on the sides of the road. The road is oriented North-South and frequently shows Babassu palms

lm.name: Infrastructure - Maceio Beach Lamp
lm.note: The large road next to the beach of Maceio has these unique lamp arms that go to one site and then cross the pole to the other side again. West of the Maceio port, they point to both sides of the road, while east of the Maceio port, they only point to one side.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Rio Branco Special Lamp
lm.note: This lamp can be found on Av. Ceara in Rio Branco.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Rio de Janeiro Landbridge
lm.note: This map west of the city of Rio de Janeiro is unique due to the water in the south, the roadlines (double yellow - double broken yellow - single broken white) and the little wall in the North. Rio mountains can be seen in most sections of the road to the North.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Serra dos Orgaos
lm.note: This road can be found North of Rio de Janeiro (city). It is a concrete road with black tar behind the road lines.

lm.name: Landscape - BR174 in Amazonas
lm.note: This road can be recognized by the Amazonian looking trees and the NW/SE angle. It always has Gen 4 and an exposed, blue car front.

lm.name: Landscape - BR230 in Amazonas
lm.note: This wide dirt road has Amazonian trees and a blurred car. You will not find other cars on the road. It's the only East-to-West angle road in that area.

lm.name: Landscape - BR230 in Para
lm.note: This road looks like an Amazonian road with the trees and dense rainforest. It runs east-west, slightly to the south. The road looks like its stained with mud

lm.name: Landscape - BR319, North of Porto Velho
lm.note: This road is characterized by it's Amazonian look and the SW-NE road angle. Some sections of this road are overcast and/or showcase a flat landscape.

lm.name: Landscape - Dunas da Sabiaguaba
lm.note: This road east of Fortaleza is characterized by its unique pavement and the sanddunes along the road.

lm.name: Landscape - Landbridge in Rio Grande do Sul
lm.note: Recognizable by the swamp-like landscape, the pine trees along the road and the Lagoon It runs at a SE-NW angle.

lm.name: Landscape - Swampy Road
lm.note: A very swampy road (PA-154) can be found Northwest of Belém. Notably, there are very few trees, and the soil is very red.

lm.name: Landscape - Uneven Stone + Corn
lm.note: This beautiful road west of Cascavel and South of Toledo, by the PR-585 is characterized by the uneven red stone pavement and the corn plantation next to it.

lm.name: Vegetation - Queen Palm
lm.note:
Queen palms have leaf stems that point upwards on the trunk and then "bow down" again to the ground due to gravity. They are native to South America. In Brazil, they are mainly found along the coast between Rio de Janeiro and Porto Alegre.

Outside of South America, they're also found in Florida and East Coast Queensland.

lm.name: Insulators - 1-top 2-alternating insulators
lm.note: Poles that have one insulator on top and alternating horizontal insulators can be found in Mato Grosso and southern Acre. It is also very rare in Rio Grande do Sul.

lm.name: Insulators - black double UFO-shaped
lm.note: Poles with these black double UFO-shaped insulators in a trident formation are common in Maranhão. The insulator itself is common across many states, but not in this configuration.

lm.name: Insulators - brown mushroom
lm.note: Insulators that resemble brown mushrooms are only found in Pernambuco.

lm.name: Insulators - dark brown insulators
lm.note: These dark brown insulators with grey bases are found almost exclusively in Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.

lm.name: Insulators - grey Lollipop
lm.note: These insulators are spherical or cone shaped and suspended on a rod above the insulator bar. They are often referred to as “lollipop” insulators. They are very common in Rio Grande de Norte, Paraíba, Pernambuco, and more rarely, Sergipe.

lm.name: Insulators - horizontal
lm.note: Poles with horizontal insulators are very common in Pará and less so in Mato Grosso. They are rarely found in Acre, Amapá, Tocantins, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.

lm.name: Insulators - long grey
lm.note:
Long grey insulators, not including when they are horizontal, are most commonly found in Pará, Mato Grosso, Tocantins, Bahia, Mato Grosso do Sul, Paraná and Santa Catarina.

They are found rarely in Maranhão, Rio Grande do Norte, Alagoas, Sergipe, Rondônia, and Rio Grande do Sul. Other states have between 0 and 5%.

lm.name: Insulators - long thin
lm.note: Insulators in Ceará can sometimes be uniquely long and thin. They are in Goiás too, but are rare.

lm.name: Insulators - spool of thread
lm.note: These insulators have a shape resembling a spool of thread. They are found mostly in Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo, and have been seen in Ceará.

lm.name: Insulators - transparent
lm.note: Transparent insulators are mostly in Alagoas in the northeast, and Santa Catarina in the south. They can be seen rarely in Sergipe, Ceará, and Brasília.

lm.name: Insulators - white mushrooms
lm.note: Insulators that resemble white mushrooms are found in Bahia and rarely Brasília.

lm.name: Marker - black paint
lm.note: Pole IDs in Paraná are usually made up of black paint and yellow or white painted text.

lm.name: Marker - long yellow paint with letter
lm.note: Markings on poles are used by the electricity companies to identify them. This pole ID is long, yellow pole paint with a black code. The ones that start with a letter are found in Bahia and Pernambuco.

lm.name: Marker - long yellow/black paint
lm.note: Similar to the Bahia and Pernambuco poles, Goiás poles also use long, yellow pole paint with a black paint code, but it always starts with a number. They also have a rarer yellow on black pole ID, which can be either paint or a plate.

lm.name: Marker - paint with street name
lm.note: Utility poles in Paraná on intersections are sometimes painted with the street name. This can sometimes extend to Santa Catarina or Rio Grande do Sul if there are ladder poles in the city.

lm.name: Marker - small beige plate with numbers
lm.note: Most poles in Maranhão have a small beige plate with numbers built into the surface of the pole. This pole ID can be found in Pará and Piauí more rarely.

lm.name: Marker - small yellow/orange plate
lm.note: This small yellow or orange plate attached onto the pole by thin metal or zip tie is found in Rio Grande do Norte and Pernambuco. This ID is usually much higher up the pole in Pernambuco than in Rio Grande do Norte.

lm.name: Marker - square yellow
lm.note: São Paulo has a square, yellow pole ID paint. It has three letters on top followed by two numbers, a black line, and four more numbers. The three letters represent the municipality within São Paulo, but are rarely visible.

lm.name: Pole - round poles
lm.note:
Alongside ladder poles, round poles can often be found across the south of Brazil, especially São Paulo. These poles are cylindrical and made of concrete.

NOTE: This map and the following wooden pole map was created using statistical analysis of semi-urban and rural locations. 434 locations of 3 poles per location were used across 16 states that were thought to have mixed poles. Regardless of the state, the centre of large cities will often have round poles.

lm.name: Pole - wooden poles
lm.note: Some states also use wooden poles. They are most commonly seen in Rio Grande do Sul, Roraima, Amazonas, and Rio de Janeiro.

lm.name: Poletop - asymmetrical crossbar with no support
lm.note:
This asymmetrical crossbar with no supports is exclusive to Ceara and Rondonia.

NOTE: While the crossbar in Ceara is usually made of concrete, the Rondonian variation features a metal crossbar, and is far less common.

lm.name: Poletop - asymmetrical crossbar with support
lm.note: This poletop, consisting of an asymmetrical crossbar and a support reaching to the middle of the longer part of the crossbar, is the most common poletop in the state of São Paulo. It can also be frequently seen in the states of Rio Grande do Sul, Rio de Janeiro and Mato Grosso do Sul.

lm.name: Poletop - electircity boxes on top
lm.note:
Gamma-shaped poles containing electricity boxes at the end of the bar are most commonly seen in the state of Rio de Janeiro and in the cities of Belém, Salvador, Fortaleza and Maceió.

NOTE: A variation with a shorter bar is exclusive to Belém.

lm.name: Poletop - João-de-Barro nests
lm.note: These spheres on top of utility poles are João-de-Barro nests. They are common across the south of Brazil.

lm.name: Poletop - pencil pole
lm.note: Poles that have a smooth cone on top, often called a pencil pole, are common in the state of Rio de Janeiro and rarely in Brasília and Manaus.

lm.name: Poletop - zig-zag top bar
lm.note: This pole configuration, featuring a zigzag-shaped top bar resting atop a flat crossbar, is exclusive to Ceara and Roraima. The pole is usually much larger than a regular electricity pole.

lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note:
• Roads in Brazil will usually feature double yellow middle lines, with white outer lines.
  • Roads can occasionally have a single dashed yellow line.

lm.name: Açai Palms
lm.note: Açai palms produce fruits that are popular globally. Most of these palms are found near Belem, but can be seen across the Amazon. They are distinct in the way the leaflets droop downward along with their unusually thin trunks.

lm.name: Babassu Palms
lm.note: Babassu palms have long, robust leaves comprised of many leaflets. Trunk length can vary from short to tall. They are found throughout the Amazon, or more rarely, down the east coast.

lm.name: Carnaúba Palms
lm.note: Carnaúba palms have short but strong, fan-like leaves and a trunk that is smooth at the top and spiked at the bottom. They are common in Ceará but are also in Piauí and Rio Grande do Norte.

lm.name: Coconut Palm Trees
lm.note:
Coconut palm trees have long leaves, can grow very tall, and have thin trunks. They are common across the north eastern states and sometimes further west or south along the coast.

NOTE: Coconut palms grow across the world and are not unique to Brazil.

lm.name: Coffee Bean Plantations
lm.note:
Coffee beans are by far the most common in Minas Gerais, but also can be found in Espírito Santo and northeastern São Paulo.

Use in combination with landscape and soil color to get a vibe for which region the coffee is from.

lm.name: Eucalyptus Grandis
lm.note: Eucalyptus Grandis, when fully grown, is a very tall tree with plantations all over Brazil. You can find them in both large and very small plantations., as well as randomly growing anywhere. You can see them all over the south, but there are some large plantations in Amapá too.

lm.name: Long Stem Plant on Roadside
lm.note: This species of plant, with long stems and many leaves growing up, are very common in Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, and Paraíba. In the dry season, you can still make out the distinct long stems without leaves.

lm.name: Macaw Palms
lm.note: Macaw palms have thin leaves compared to other palms, and often have a visible spear shaped top. They are very common around Mato Grosso do Sul and the surrounding states, but can be seen much further out sometimes. These palms should be used with caution, and single trees are much less of an indicator than multiple trees.

lm.name: Moriche Palms
lm.note:
Moriche palms have leaves with a rounded fan shape. They are most common in Amazonas, Acre, and Roraima, but can be found in all of the Amazonian states.

NOTE: These palms can additionally be found very commonly in the Amazonian parts of Colombia and Peru.

lm.name: Paraná Pines
lm.note: These distinct trees, called Paraná pines, have long horizontal branches with leaves only at the end. They grow mainly in the southern Brazilian states of Paraná, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul.

lm.name: Soybeans
lm.note: Soybeans appear as small, leafy soil grown plants. They are most commonly grown in Mato Grosso, Paraná, and Goiás.

lm.name: Sugarcane Plantations
lm.note:
Sugarcane plantations are by far most common in the state of São Paulo, and in the coastal north east states, especially Alagoas and Pernambuco.

As a rule of thumb: The sugarcane plantations in the south will more often have red soil, while the ones in Alagoas and Pernambuco will be more yellow/white.

lm.name: Tocantins Grass
lm.note: Very tall grass can be often seen in the centre of the country, most notably in the Tocantins, Goiás, Bahia, and Minas Gerais states.

lm.name: Pole - wooden poles
lm.note: Some states also use wooden poles. They are most commonly seen in Rio Grande do Sul, Roraima, Amazonas, and Rio de Janeiro.

lm.name: Poletop - asymmetrical crossbar with no support
lm.note:
This asymmetrical crossbar with no supports is exclusive to Ceara and Rondonia.

NOTE: While the crossbar in Ceara is usually made of concrete, the Rondonian variation features a metal crossbar, and is far less common.

top.html:
Soil in most of Brazil is distinctly red. It can range from a light pink around Mato Grosso to a deep maroon near the Paraná river. The soil is usually not red in the North East, or in the majority of Rio Grande do Sul, however.

NOTE: Parts of Paraguay and the nearby Argentine province of Misiones have deep red soil, as well a handful of other regions around the world.

The soil is usually not red in the North East, or in the majority of Rio Grande do Sul, however.
